questions.domain: Inflation, Interest Rates, and the Economy
questions.prompt: Rosa's savings earn 4.5% a year and inflation is 3%. About what is her real rate of return?
questions.intro: The nominal rate is the stated rate. The real rate shows growth in buying power: real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation rate.
sources: Federal Reserve (Monetary policy): The Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate to pursue maximum employment and stable prices; it has a longer-run inflation goal of 2%. (https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm)

questions.domain: Inflation, Interest Rates, and the Economy
questions.prompt: Rosa gets a 2% raise when inflation is 4%. What happens to her real pay?
questions.intro: Real pay change ≈ raise − inflation. If prices rise faster than pay, the same paycheck buys less.

questions.domain: Inflation, Interest Rates, and the Economy
questions.prompt: When the Federal Reserve raises its target interest rate, what usually happens to loan rates?

choices.text: They stay the same until each loan ends
They are unaffected; only savings rates change

questions.intro: The Federal Reserve sets a target for the federal funds rate, which banks charge each other overnight. Changes ripple to credit card, auto, and mortgage rates and to savings yields. Raising rates tends to slow borrowing and cool inflation.
questions.feedback: Higher Fed rates push borrowing costs up.

misconceptions.C: Confuses new loans with fixed loans
